```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
library(tidyverse)
# tutorial_options(exercise.timelimit = 60)

countries_data <- data.frame(
  Country = c("Canada", "Japan", "Brazil", "Egypt", "Germany", "Australia"),
  Capital = c("Ottawa", "Tokyo", "Brasília", "Cairo", "Berlin", "Canberra"),
  Continent = c("North America", "Asia", "South America", "Africa", "Europe", "Oceania")
)

school <- data.frame(Age = 1:18,
                     School = c("Preschool", "Preschool","Preschool","Preschool", "Preschool",
                              "Primary school", "Primary school","Primary school","Primary school",
                              "Middle school","Middle school","Middle school","Middle school","Middle school","Middle school", "High school", "High school", "High school"))
```

## Introduction

This interactive tutorial will guide you through common **dplyr** and base R functions for data manipulation. You will practice with real datasets like `mtcars`, `iris`, `starwars`, and `airquality`.

#### mtcars

The **`mtcars`** dataset contains car data with fuel consumption and design specs for 32 car models taken from the US magazine *Motor Trend* (1973–74).

| Column | Explanation |
| ----- | ---- |
| `mpg` |     Miles/(US) gallon |
| `cyl` |     Number of cylinders |
| `disp` |    Displacement (cu.in.) |
| `hp` |  Gross horsepower |
| `drat` |    Rear axle ratio |
| `wt` |  Weight (1000 lbs) |
| `qsec` |    1/4 mile time |
| `vs` |  Engine (0 = V-shaped, 1 = straight) |
| `am` |  Transmission (0 = automatic, 1 = manual) |
| `gear` |    Number of forward gears  |

#### iris

The **`iris`** dataset contains measurements (sepal/petal) of 150 iris flowers across three species. Originally published by [the  UCI Machine Learning Repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/53/iris).

| Column | Explanation |
| ----- | ---- |
|`Sepal.Length` | Length of sepals  |
|`Sepal.Width` | Width of sepals   |
|`Petal.Length` | Length of petals |
|`Petal.Width` | Width of petals |
|`Species`| One of 3 species |

![Flower diagram from Wikipedia](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7f/Mature_flower_diagram.svg){width=70%}

#### starwars

The **`starwars`** dataset from the `dplyr` package contains [data on characters from the Star Wars universe](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/starwars.html).

| Column | Explanation |
| ----- | ---- |
| `name` |     Name of the character |
| `height` |  Height (cm) |
| `mass` |     Weight (kg) |
| `hair_color`, `skin_color`, `eye_color` | Hair, skin, and eye colors |
| `birth_year` | Year born (BBY = Before Battle of Yavin)
| `sex` | The biological sex of the character, namely male, female, hermaphroditic, or none (as in the case for Droids). |
| `gender` |     The gender role or gender identity of the character as determined by their personality or the way they were programmed (as in the case for Droids). |
| `homeworld` |     Name of homeworld | 
| `species` | Name of species |
| `films` | List of films the character appeared in |
| `vehicles` | List of vehicles the character has piloted |
| `starships` | List of starships the character has piloted |


#### airquality

The **`airquality`** data contains daily air quality measurements in New York (May–September 1973).
   
| Column | Explanation |
| ----- | ---- |
| `Ozone` | Mean ozone in parts per billion from 1300 to 1500 hours at Roosevelt Island |
| `Solar.R`|  Solar radiation in Langleys in the frequency band 4000–7700 Angstroms from 0800 to 1200 hours at Central Park |
| `Wind` | Average wind speed in miles per hour at 0700 and 1000 hours at LaGuardia Airport |
| `Temp` | Maximum daily temperature in degrees Fahrenheit at La Guardia Airport. |

## 1. Working directory

A directory or folder is a container for storing files or other folders. This is where R will look for files, where R will save visible and hidden files, and where R will automatically load files from.

*4 exercises*

```{r packages-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here
```

### Exercise 2.3: Unload packages

Sometimes packages will conflict with one another. Then you might want to "unload" a packages. Unload the packages you just installed and loaded into the workspace.

```{r packages-ex3, exercise=TRUE}

```

```{r packages-ex3-solution}

# Option 2

detach("package:formattable", unload = TRUE)
```


## 6. `filter()`

*7 exercises*

Filtering rows is analogous to selecting columns. Some rows are not relevant to us (or maybe at all!) and removing them makes it easier to determine the important information.

In class, we spoke about using R as a calculator and how it can do basic functions:

| Function                               | Symbol              |
|:---------------------------------------|---------------------|
| addition                               | `+`                 |
| subtraction                            | `-`                 |
| division                               | `/`                 |
| multiplication                         | `*`                 |
| power                                  | `^`                 |
| equals                                 | `==`                |
| does not equal                         | `!=`                |
| greater than                           | `>`                 |
| greater than or equal                  | `>=`                |
| less than                              | `<`                 |
| less than or equal                     | `<=`                |
| range (from NR1 to NR2)                | NR1`:`NR2           |
| identify element (is VALUE in OBJECT?) | VALUE `%in%` OBJECT |

We also practiced set theory. 
**Set theory** is a part of math and a way to thinking about groups of things and how they relate to each other. These "things" can be anything: numbers, letters, shapes, people, concepts, ideas, etc. We call these collections sets and each thing inside the set is called an **element**. Sets are useful because they allow us to analyze arguments using logic and structure, define categories (e.g. all living beings) and compare them ("some living beings are humans"). You can combine and compare sets by using unions ('or' `|`, so everything in A or B) and intersections ('and' `&`, so only what is in *both* A and B).


![Venn diagram from slides in Week 4](https://pryslopska.com/img/venn-logic.png){width=50%}

### Exercise 6.1: Basic filtering

Filter `mtcars` for rows where the miles per gallon are more than 25.

```{r filter-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex1-solution}
filter(mtcars, mpg > 25)
```

### Exercise 6.2: Multiple conditions

From `starwars`, keep only masculine characters which are taller than 180.

```{r filter-ex2, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex2-solution}
filter(starwars, gender == 'masculine', height > 180)
```

### Exercise 6.3: Filter with %in%

On `iris`, filter only the setosa and versicolor species.

```{r filter-ex3, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```


```{r filter-ex3-solution}
filter(iris, Species %in% c('setosa', 'versicolor'))
```

### Exercise 6.4: More filters 

On `iris`, how many flowers of the virginica species have the petal width of at least 2.5 and petal length of 6 or less?

```{r filter-ex4, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```


```{r filter-ex4-solution}
# This is true of only 2 flowers
filter(iris, Species == 'virginica',
       Petal.Width > 2.4,
       Petal.Length <= 6.0) 
```

### Exercise 6.5: Mixing filters

Look at the `starwars` data. What is the name and species of the man who is between 100 and 180 cm tall, has black or blue eyes, weighs 80 kg or less, does not have black hair, and whose homeworld is neither "Sullust" nor "Bespin".

```{r filter-ex5, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```


```{r filter-ex5-solution}
filter(starwars, 
       sex == "male",
       height %in% 100:180,
       eye_color %in% c("black", "blue"),
       mass <= 80,
       hair_color != "black",
       !(homeworld %in% c("Sullust", "Bespin")))
```

<div>
**Hint:** You don't need to select the name and species. It's enough if you return the row with this individual.
</div>


### Exercise 6.6: More mixing filters

Look at the `starwars` data.  What is the homeworld of the grey or green-skinned, bald man, who has neither yellow nor gold eyes. They weigh under 90 kg and don't pilot the Millennium Falcon. They're either over 230 cm or under 200 cm tall.

```{r filter-ex6, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex6-solution}
filter(starwars,
       skin_color %in% c("grey", "green"),
       hair_color == "none",
       sex =="male",
       !(eye_color %in% c("yellow", "gold")),
       mass < 90,
       starships != "Millennium Falcon",
       (height < 200 | height > 230)) 
```

<div>
**Hint:** You don't need to select the homeworld. It's enough if you return the row with this individual.
</div>

### Exercise 6.7: Even more filters

Look at the `starwars` data. Find the only woman with a combined height and mass under 200.

```{r filter-ex7, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex7-solution}
filter(starwars,
       sex =="female",
       (height + mass) < 200) 
```

## 7. `mutate()`

*3 exercises*

In R, mutating means adding new columns or changing existing ones in a dataframe. 

### Exercise 7.1: Create a new column

In `mtcars`, make a new column called "power_to_weight" which is the ratio of horse power to weight.

```{r mutate-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here


```

```{r mutate-ex1-solution}
mutate(mtcars, power_to_weight = hp / wt)
```

<div>

**Hint:** To calculate the ratio you need to divide one thing by the other. Check the column names in the code window or in the introduction to figure out which values you need.

</div>


### Exercise 7.2: Multiple mutations

In `starwars`, calculate two values:

- "height_m" each character's height in meters, and
- "bmi" [the body mass index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_mass_index) of each character.

**Don't use pipes for this exercise.**

```{r mutate-ex2, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here



```

<div>

**Hint 1:** BMI is measured in kg/m2. The "height" values in `starwars` are in centimeters.

**Hint 2:** Since we're not using pipes at this stage yet, you have to proceed in 2 steps.

</div>


```{r mutate-ex2-solution}
starwars <- mutate(starwars, height_m = height / 100)
starwars <- mutate(starwars, bmi = mass / (height_m ^ 2))
```

### Exercise 7.3: More mutations

Convert temperature from Fahrenheit to Celsius in `airquality` data and save it to a new column "temp_c".

```{r mutate-ex3, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r mutate-ex3-solution}
mutate(airquality, temp_c = (Temp - 32) * 5 / 9)
```

<div>

**Hint:** The conversion formula is temperature °C =  (temperature °F - 32) * 5/9

</div>

## 8. `na.omit()`

*7 exercises*

There are many ways in which you can deal with missing values, which is what R calls `NA`. You can remove them (which is what we're doing here), set them to a specific value, or other things. In class, we simply removed all NAs. As a rule of thumb, you want to look at what values are missing from your data to see if there is anything amiss with it.

This function takes only one argument.

### Exercise 8.1: Remove rows with any NA

Apply `na.omit()` to `airquality` and report the number of rows before and after.

```{r naomit-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r naomit-ex1-solution}
nrow(airquality)
nrow(na.omit(airquality))
```

<div>

**Hint:** Use the function `nrow()` to get the number of rows of a dataframe.

</div>

### Exercise 8.2: Compare before and after

Report the number of rows of the `starwars` data before and after removing missing values.

```{r naomit-ex2, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here


```

```{r naomit-ex2-solution}
nrow(starwars)
nrow(na.omit(starwars))
```

### Exercise 8.3: Difference

Subtract the number of rows with missing values from the number of all rows in the `iris` dataset.

```{r naomit-ex3, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r naomit-ex3-solution}
nrow(iris) - nrow(na.omit(iris))
```


### Exercise 8.4: Chain with select

In the `starwars` data, remove NAs then select the name, weight, and birth_year.
**Do this in two steps.**

```{r naomit-ex4, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```


```{r naomit-ex4-solution}
df1 <- na.omit(starwars) 
select(df1, name, mass, birth_year)
```

### Exercise 8.5: Show all missing values

Using and `filter()`, show all the rows in the `airquality` dataset with missing values.

```{r naomit-ex5, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```


```{r naomit-ex5-solution}
filter(airquality, is.na(Ozone)==TRUE)
```

<div>

**Hint:** Use the function `is.na()` to get a logical vector of rows with an `NA` value. This is similar to the functions `is.numeric()`, `is.logical()` etc. that we talked out in class.

</div>

### Exercise 8.6: Chain with select in one line

In the `airquality` data, remove NAs then select the the wind and temperature.
**Do this in one steps and one line.**

```{r naomit-ex6, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```


```{r naomit-ex6-solution}
select(na.omit(airquality), Wind, Temp)
```

<div>

**Hint:** You can nest functions, which means calling one function from inside another function.

</div>


### Exercise 8.7: Chain multiple functions in one line

In the `airquality` data, remove NAs then select the the wind and temperature, then count the number of rows.
**Do this in one steps and one line.**

```{r naomit-ex7, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```


```{r naomit-ex7-solution}
nrow(select(na.omit(airquality), Wind, Temp))
```

<div>

**Hint:** You can the `nrow()` functions to return the number of rows.

</div>

## 11. Pipes

*7 exercises*

A powerful tool for clearly expressing a sequence of multiple
operations. Passes the output as the new input. They can be read as
"and then".

The pipe translates `x |> f(y)` into `f(x, y)`.


### Exercise 11.1: Use |> with select

Select name and species from `starwars` using native pipe.

```{r pipe-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```  

```{r pipe-ex1-solution}
starwars |> select(name, species)
```

### Exercise 11.2: Use |> with select

Remove only the skin color from `starwars` using native pipe.

```{r pipe-ex2, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```  

```{r pipe-ex2-solution}
starwars |> select(-skin_color)
```


### Exercise 11.3: Combine filter and select

Filter only the hermaphroditic characters from `starwars` and select their name, skin color and eye color. 

```{r pipe-ex3, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```  

```{r pipe-ex3-solution}
starwars |> 
  filter(sex == "hermaphroditic")  |>
  select(name, skin_color, eye_color)
```


### Exercise 11.4: Pipeline with filter, select and mutate

Filter only the female characters from `starwars` and select all the columns except for their hair color. Then change their height to meters.


```{r pipe-ex4, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here


```

```{r pipe-ex4-solution}
starwars |> 
  filter(sex == "female")  |>
  select(-hair_color) |>
  mutate(height = height/100)
```


### Exercise 11.5: Pipeline with filter, select, remove missing values, and mutate

From the `airquality` dataset, filter the data from June, drop the day of the month, remove missing values, and change the temperature from °Fahrenheit to °Celsius.


```{r pipe-ex5, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here




```

```{r pipe-ex5-solution}
airquality |>
  filter(Month == 6) |>
  select(-Day) |>
  na.omit() |>
  mutate(Temp = (Temp - 32) * 5/9)
```

<div>

**Hint:** The conversion formula is temperature °C =  (temperature °F - 32) * 5/9

</div>


### Exercise 11.6: Pipeline with filter, select, remove missing values, mutate, and arrange

From the `airquality` dataset, filter the data from the first three weeks of August, keep only the columns "Ozone", "Solar.R", "Wind", and "Temp", remove missing values, change the temperature from °Fahrenheit to °Celsius, change the wind speed from miles per hour to kilometers per hour, make a new column "Month" with the name of the month in English, and sort the values by ozone (ascending) and solar radiation (descending).


```{r pipe-ex6, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here




```

```{r pipe-ex6-solution}
airquality |>
  filter(Month == 8,
         Day <22) |>
  select(Ozone, Solar.R, Wind, Temp) |>
  na.omit() |>
  mutate(Temp = (Temp - 32) * 5/9,
         Wind = Wind * 1609.344,
         Month = "August") |>
  arrange(Ozone, -Solar.R)
```

<div>

**Hint:** One mile is around 1609.344 meters.

</div>


### Exercise 11.7: Pipeline with filter, select, remove missing values, and mutate

From the `airquality` dataset, filter the data from May, remove missing values, change the temperature from °Fahrenheit to °Celsius, round the resulting temperature to a whole number (no decimal points), and return only the unique temperatures.   filter(Month == 5) |>
```{r pipe-ex7-solution}
  na.omit() |>
  mutate(Temp = round((Temp - 32) * 5/9), 0) |>
  select(Temp) |>
  unique() |>

```

<div>

**Hint 1:** Use the `round()` function to round a number. It takes two arguments: values (a number or a numeric vector, like a column) and number of decimal places (default 0).

**Hint 2:** Use `nrow()` to return the number of rows.

</div>

## 12. Grouping and summarizing

*8 + 2 exercises*


When you group data with `group_by()`, you're putting it into categories based on one or more columns (like grouping people by age or cars by number of cylinders). Calling the grouping function does not change anything *visibly* but it changes the data "under the hood".

When you summarize with `summarize()`, you calculate some new values for each group—like the average, total, or count. `summarize()` calculates a single value (per group) and drops columns which are not grouped by. In contrast, `mutate()` changes an existing column or adds a new one, but does not drop columns.

**Use pipes to solve these exercises.**

Recall that in Week 3 of the course we talked about the measures of central tendency (mean, median, standard deviation etc.). If you get stuck on these exercises, check the handout for week 3, pages 22-24.

## 13. If else statements

*8 exercises*

In class, we used `ifelse()` and `case_when()` to recode values for conditions and also validate the answers to the Moses illusion questions.

- Use `ifelse()` when you have one condition (or maybe two). It’s great for simple either/or decisions.
- Use `case_when()` when you have multiple conditions. It checks several conditions in order, and returns the first one that's true.

**Remember to use pipes to solve these exercises.**

![Diagram of an if else statement](https://pryslopska.com/img/ifelse.png){width=50%}

Label the cars in `mtcars` with a speed class based on horse power: "High" for over 150 horse power, "Medium" for over 100 horse power, and "Low" otherwise. Use `case_when()`, because you have 3 options.

## 14. Assignment and Data Input

In R, you can use three operators to assign values to a variable: `->`, `=`, and `->>`. 

| Operator | Example | Uses |
| -------- | ------- | ---- |
| `<-` and `->` | `x <- 5` | This is the traditional way of assigning values. You can read it as "Put 5 in x". |
| `=` | `x = 5` | This is similar to the operator above. It works fine in most cases and is usually used inside functions (like `nrow(x = starwars)`). You can read the example as "Set x equal to 5". |
| `->>` and `<<-` | `x <<- 5` | This is a special kind of `<-` operator: a "global assignment" operator. It assigns 5 to x in the **global environment** (outside the local scope), even if you're inside a function. In lay terms, it makes the variable jump out of its environment and become global.|

In this course, we use the `->` operator for assigning global values (e.g. outside of functions) and the `=` operator for assigning values inside functions.

```{r, echo=FALSE, include=TRUE}
starwars_rows <- nrow(x = starwars)
```

### Exercise 15.4: Combining data with `cbind()`

Think of `cbind()` as adding more columns to your data.
Use it when you're adding new types of information about your existing entries (like currency and timezone). It is used to bind any number of dataframes by column. The resulting dataframe is wider.

In this exercise, you will create two new variables called `Population` and  `Official_Language` with the population and official languages of these countries. Then, use `cbind()` to add first "Population" and then "Official_Language" to the dataframe. The first part of the code is provided for you. Save the resulting the dataframe by overwriting `countries_data` and preview the data.

|  Country  | Capital |     Continent |   Population |     Official_Language |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
|   Canada  |   Ottawa | North America |    39.566 | English and French |
|    Japan  |    Tokyo |          Asia |   123.199 |             Japanese |
|   Brazil  |Brasília | South America |    212.693 |          Portuguese |
|    Egypt  |    Cairo |        Africa |   118.084 |               Arabic |
|  Germany  |   Berlin |        Europe |   84.145 |               German |
| Australia |  Canberra |      Oceania  | 26.934 |               English |


```{r cbind1, exercise=TRUE}
countries_data <- data.frame(
  Country = c("Canada", "Japan", "Brazil", "Egypt", "Germany", "Australia"),
  Capital = c("Ottawa", "Tokyo", "Brasília", "Cairo", "Berlin", "Canberra"),
  Continent = c("North America", "Asia", "South America", "Africa", "Europe", "Oceania")
)

Population = c(39.566, 123.199, 212.693, 118.084, 84.145, 26.934)
countries_data <- cbind(countries_data, Population)

# Write your code here 

```

```{r cbind1-solution}

  Country = c("Canada", "Japan", "Brazil", "Egypt", "Germany", "Australia"),
  Capital = c("Ottawa", "Tokyo", "Brasília", "Cairo", "Berlin", "Canberra"),
  Continent = c("North America", "Asia", "South America", "Africa", "Europe", "Oceania")
)
```

```{r crbind1-solution, exercise=TRUE}
  Capital = "Nairobi",
  Continent = "Africa",
  Population = 57.372,
  Official_Language = "English, Swahili"
)

mexico <- data.frame(
  Country = c("Mexico"),
  Capital = c("Mexico City"),
  Continent = c("North America"),
  Population  = c(128.932),
  Official_Language  = NA)

# New columns
currency    <- c(
  "CAD", "JPY", "BRL", "EGP", "EUR", "AUD", "PLN", "XPF", "INR", "PEN", "KES", "MXN")

timezone    <- c(
  "UTC-05:00", # Canada (Ottawa)
  "UTC+09:00", # Japan (Tokyo)
  "UTC-03:00", # Brazil (Brasília)
  "UTC+02:00", # Egypt (Cairo)
  "UTC+01:00", # Germany (Berlin)
  "UTC+10:00", # Australia (Canberra)
  "UTC+01:00", # Poland (Warsaw)
  "UTC-10:00", # French Polynesia (Papeete)
  "UTC+05:30", # India (New Delhi)
  "UTC−05:00", # Peru (Lima)
  "UTC+03:00", # Kenya (Nairobi)
  "UTC-06:00"  # Mexico (Mexico City)
)

calling_code <- c(
  "+1", "+81", "+55", "+20", "+49", "+61", "+48", "+689", "+91", "+51", "+254", "+52")

# Adding the four new countries.
countries_data <- rbind(countries_data,
                        india, 
                        peru,
                        kenya,
                        mexico)

# Adding the four new rows.
countries_data <- cbind(countries_data,
                        Currency = currency,
                        Timezone = timezone,
                        Calling_code = calling_code)
                        

contries_final <- arrange(countries_data, 
                          Continent, 
                          -Population,
                          Timezone)
contries_final
```

## 16. Joining Data

*10 exercises*

Sometimes, you have two dataframes, and you want to combine them based on something they have in common (e.g. matching people by name, countries by continent, or books by title and author). `merge()` is a built-in R function. It looks for a common column (like "Country") in two dataframes and joins the rows that match. The `dplyr` package gives you more precise control with functions like:

- `left_join()`
- `right_join()`
- `inner_join()`
- `full_join()`
- `anti_join()`

They all do the same basic thing as `merge()`: combine two dataframes using a shared column. But they let you choose what to keep if there's not a perfect match.

![Venn diagram from slides in Week 5](https://pryslopska.com/img/venn-join.png){width=50%}

### Exercise 16.1: Full join two small dataframes

For this exercise, do the following tasks:

1. Create a dataframe with names of 10 children **in this order** (Lila, Kai, Ezra, Maya, Ethan, Zoe, Leo, Isla, Raja, Zara) and their ages (7, 2, 12, 4, 3, 2, 10, 13, 6, 7), assign it to `children`.
2. Create a second dataframe with the names of the children  **in this order** (Zoe, Kai, Lila, Ethan, Leo, Ezra, Isla, Zara, Maya, Raja) and their favorite animals (Clownfish, Panda, Elephant, Penguin, Koala, Tiger, Giraffe, Rabbit, Cat, Fox), assign it to `animals`.
3. Use `full_join()` to join these two dataframes by the common identifier column.

```{r joinpractice-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here 

```

```{r joinpractice-ex1-solution}
children <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Lila", "Kai", "Ezra", "Maya", "Ethan", "Zoe", "Leo", "Isla", "Raja", "Zara"),
  Age = c(7, 2, 12, 4, 3, 2, 10, 13, 6, 7))

animals <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Zoe", "Kai", "Lila", "Ethan", "Leo", "Ezra", "Isla", "Zara", "Maya", "Raja"),
  Animal = c("Clownfish", "Panda", "Elephant", "Penguin", "Koala", "Tiger", "Giraffe", "Rabbit", "Cat", "Fox"))

full_join(children, animals, by="Name")
```

<div>

**Hint:** The `full_join()` function takes as argument two dataframes and the common identifier arguments by which to match the rows `by=`.

</div>

### Exercise 16.8: Add missing ages and schools

When using `full_join()` on the `children` and `animals` dataframes, there were ages missing from a few kids. In this exercise you will:

1. Create a dataframe for children and their favorite animals (this code is provided for you).
2. Use `full_join()` to create a combined dataframe of `children` and `animals`.
3. Using `case_when()`, add the ages for Catherine (5), Takeshi and Sven (both 8), Anouk (3), and Amara (11).
4. Then, create a new column called `School` for the school they go to:
  - 1-5: Preschool
  - 6-9: Primary school
  - 10-15: Middle school
  - 16+: High school
5. Calculate the number of children (`N`) and their average age (`Mean_age`) per school.
6. Sort the results by number of children.
7. Print the resulting dataframe.

**Use pipes to complete steps 2-7.**

```{r joinpractice-ex8, exercise=TRUE} 
children <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Lila", "Kai", "Ezra", "Maya", "Ethan", "Zoe", "Leo", "Isla", "Raja", "Zara"),
  Age = c(7, 2, 12, 4, 3, 2, 10, 13, 6, 7))

animals <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Zoe", "Kai", "Lila", "Ethan", "Leo", "Ezra", "Isla", "Zara", "Maya", "Raja", "Catherine", "Takeshi", "Sven", "Anouk", "Amara"),
  Favorite_Animal = c("Clownfish", "Panda", "Elephant", "Penguin", "Koala", "Tiger", "Giraffe", "Rabbit", "Cat", "Fox", "Dog", "Otter", "Parrot", "Owl", "Llama"))

###################################
# Start your code here
###################################


```


```{r joinpractice-ex8-solution, exercise=TRUE} 
children <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Lila", "Kai", "Ezra", "Maya", "Ethan", "Zoe", "Leo", "Isla", "Raja", "Zara"),
  Age = c(7, 2, 12, 4, 3, 2, 10, 13, 6, 7))

animals <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Zoe", "Kai", "Lila", "Ethan", "Leo", "Ezra", "Isla", "Zara", "Maya", "Raja", "Catherine", "Takeshi", "Sven", "Anouk", "Amara"),
  Favorite_Animal = c("Clownfish", "Panda", "Elephant", "Penguin", "Koala", "Tiger", "Giraffe", "Rabbit", "Cat", "Fox", "Dog", "Otter", "Parrot", "Owl", "Llama"))


full_join(children, animals, by = "Name") |>
  mutate(
    Age = case_when(
      Name == "Catherine" ~ 5,
      Name == "Takeshi" ~ 8,
      Name == "Sven" ~ 8,
      Name == "Anouk" ~ 3,
      Name == "Amara" ~ 11,
      TRUE ~ Age           # Keep everything else as it is.
    ),
    School = case_when(
      Age >= 1 & Age <= 5 ~ "Preschool",
      Age >= 6 & Age <= 9 ~ "Primary school",
      Age >= 10 & Age <= 15 ~ "Middle school",
      TRUE ~ "Highschool"
    )) |>
  group_by(School) |>
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean_Age = mean(Age)
  ) |>
  arrange(N)

```

<div>

**Hint:** Think about how to handle the cases where you **don't** want to change the age.

</div>
